summary:
Developed by IPM Mecs, a team of young engineering students from Barranquilla, Colombia, MissionLab allows users to design and evaluate virtual space missions by making engineering decisions involving scientific objectives, spacecraft systems, payload selection, propulsion, energy management, communications, and mission budgets.

The platform combines scientific concepts, mathematical models, and a game-based learning experience inspired by NASA's space systems engineering methodology.
details:
Feel inspired to dig into research!

Every space mission begins with an idea, but transforming that idea into a feasible mission requires much more than imagination. Engineers must balance scientific objectives, technological capabilities, limited resources, and interconnected systems. MissionLab was created to bring that decision-making process closer to students, enthusiasts, and the next generation of space explorers.

Space mission design also involves complex engineering concepts that can be difficult for beginners to understand. Many educational resources explain these concepts theoretically but offer limited opportunities to explore how engineering decisions affect an entire mission.

Our goal is to make aerospace engineering more accessible through experimentation, problem-solving, and game-based learning.

MissionLab provides a bilingual (English and Spanish) web-based simulation on NASA's Design and Develop Science Missions educational resource.

  • Mission Selection: Choose scientific objectives and mission scenarios.
  • Spacecraft Design: Select instruments, payloads, and spacecraft subsystems.
  • Engineering Simulation: Evaluate simplified models involving spacecraft mass, delta-v, power, thermal conditions, communications, and mission costs.
  • Requirements Verification: Identify whether selected configurations satisfy scientific and engineering constraints.

Design Your Own Space Mission

MissionLab guides users through an interactive engineering design process, beginning with the selection of a mission and its scientific objectives. Users then configure their spacecraft by choosing scientific instruments and onboard systems, while adjusting parameters related to propulsion, orbital requirements, electrical power, thermal conditions, and communications.

Once the configuration is complete, the simulator evaluates the design against predefined engineering requirements, identifying technical limitations and providing recommendations. Users can modify their decisions, compare results, and refine their mission through an iterative learning process.

Learning Through Engineering Trade-offs

In engineering, designing a successful mission requires balancing competing technical requirements rather than simply maximizing individual capabilities. Every engineering decision involves trade-offs: increasing the performance of one subsystem may demand additional resources or negatively affect another. The optimal configuration is not necessarily the most powerful or expensive one, but the one that best satisfies the specific requirements and priorities of the mission.

To explore these engineering trade-offs, MissionLab evaluates interconnected variables across several systems:

  • Propulsion and orbital requirements: Delta-v budgets and conceptual orbital transfers influence the mission's maneuvering capabilities and propulsion needs.
  • Electrical systems: Power generation and consumption must remain balanced to support scientific instruments and onboard equipment.
  • Thermal performance: Operating temperatures must stay within acceptable limits to maintain subsystem functionality.
  • Communications: Link budgets and signal margins determine whether the modeled communication requirements are satisfied.
  • Mission resources: Spacecraft mass and estimated costs impose constraints that influence equipment selection and overall design feasibility.

Our Vision

MissionLab aims to make the engineering process behind space exploration understandable and engaging for students worldwide.

Our future vision includes Amateur Rocketry Lab, an educational extension connecting documented model-rocketry experiences with space mission design concepts.

As first-time hackathon participants, we want to learn, experiment, and establish a foundation for future aerospace education projects.
